patterns.title: Credible Commitment
patterns.domain: Information, incentive, and commitment problems; sequential strategic choices, payment control, enforcement, and self-commitment

sources.title: Thomas C. Schelling, An Essay on Bargaining (1956)
sources.supports: Foundational strategic self-binding, visible changes in incentives or discretion, contingent threats, and institutional and renegotiation limits on contractual commitments.
sources.read_method: University-hosted original paper opened and read in full-text extraction: introductory definition, bargaining power and third-party commitment examples, observability, renegotiation, and the threat section. Publication metadata checked on the original scan.
sources.boundary: The article attributes a foundational analysis rather than inventorship of all commitment practices. No direct quotation or recommendation of destructive bargaining tactics. Ira and Sam’s payment game is an original teaching model, not Schelling’s house-price example.

sources.title: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott, Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans (1977)
sources.supports: Formal policy time inconsistency with rational expectations and a fixed objective; anticipation of later choices changes earlier private decisions.
sources.read_method: Original paper opened and read in university-hosted full-text extraction after an alternate scan yielded no text. Introduction, two-period framing, patent example, stated inflation/unemployment assumptions, and consistency/expectations discussion read.
sources.boundary: Conditional theoretical results, not an empirical universal claim that rules outperform discretion. No macroeconomic parameter, contemporary policy recommendation, or proof verification is asserted.

sources.title: Nava Ashraf, Dean Karlan, and Wesley Yin, Tying Odysseus to the Mast: Evidence from a Commitment Savings Product in the Philippines (2006)
sources.supports: Original randomized field experiment offering a savings product restricting withdrawals to a goal date or balance; voluntary take-up, higher average bank savings at twelve months for the offered group, and accompanying goal-oriented features.
sources.read_method: Published QJE paper opened and read: abstract, introduction, product design and exceptions, deposit/goal features, randomization and survey sample, and reported twelve-month intent-to-treat result.
sources.boundary: The article reports direction, not effect size, and correctly concerns assignment to an offer rather than all account openers. It does not identify restrictions separately from every bundled feature, infer individual welfare gains, claim universal adoption, extrapolate beyond twelve months, or test the hypothetical camera-sale commitment mechanism.

patterns.short_description: Make future promises dependable by changing control, available choices, or the consequences of reversal before another party becomes vulnerable.
use_when: Who controls payment after satisfactory delivery?
goals: Recognize the familiar situation and preserve the defining mechanism.
Distinguish formal assumptions, empirical findings, and hypothetical continuations.
Make intervention authority, opportunity costs, and remaining constraints explicit.
mechanisms: Reserve payment under reliable independent control before dispatch, with clear release and failure rules.
No named platform is modeled. Satisfactory delivery must be verifiable; secure later payment does not fund earlier costs.

example_structure.scenario: Hypothetical online camera sale contrasts seller dispatch before unsecured later payment with independent reservation before dispatch and conditional release after verified satisfactory delivery. Own-material one-shot benchmark excludes effective recovery, intrinsic honesty, and future dealings. Reliable custody, verification, failure/dispute rules, fees, acceptance, and earlier packing/postage finance are required. No named platform terms or guarantee of working goods is asserted.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Reserve payment under reliable independent control before dispatch, with clear release and failure rules.
example_structure.residual_constraints: No named platform is modeled. Satisfactory delivery must be verifiable; secure later payment does not fund earlier costs.
example_structure.comparison: Qualitative choices, dependencies, and consequences; no invented scores, computed trajectory, or measured improvement claimed.

visual.question: Who controls payment after satisfactory delivery?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. In the unsecured sale Ira sends the camera before Sam chooses whether to pay. In the revised arrangement an independent holder reserves payment before dispatch and releases it after verified satisfactory delivery. Sam cannot unilaterally divert that payment; Ira still funds earlier costs. Change: Reserve payment under reliable independent control before dispatch, with clear release and failure rules. Limitation: No named platform is modeled. Satisfactory delivery must be verifiable; secure later payment does not fund earlier costs.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. The lower sequence changes later control, rather than relying on a stronger promise. Payment release is conditional on the defined delivery test. Custody, verification, disputes, tied-up money, and packing or postage finance remain real constraints.
